questions.question: Explain what the Cradle of Humankind is and how fossils formed there.
questions.expected_answer: The Cradle of Humankind is an area mainly in Gauteng, north-west of Johannesburg, with a small part in North West, and a World Heritage Site since 1999. Water dissolved its dolomite rock to form caves. Over millions of years, bones of animals and early human ancestors fell or were carried into the caves, were covered by sand and stones and hardened into rock, preserving them as fossils.

questions.question: Describe three famous discoveries made in the Cradle of Humankind.
questions.expected_answer: Mrs Ples, found at Sterkfontein in 1947 by Robert Broom and John Robinson, is a skull of an Australopithecus more than two million years old. Little Foot, found at Sterkfontein in 1997 by Stephen Motsumi and Nkwane Molefe, is an almost complete skeleton, millions of years old. Homo naledi, found in the Rising Star Cave in 2013 by a team led by Lee Berger, is a new kind of human relative.

questions.question: Why is the Cradle of Humankind heritage for all humanity?
questions.expected_answer: Fossils from the Cradle and other parts of Africa show that the earliest human ancestors lived in Africa and that modern humans first appeared in Africa before spreading to other continents. So every person on Earth has ancestors who lived in Africa, and the Cradle tells the story of where all people come from, showing our common origin.
